Overview: Iowa Lieutenant Governor Chris Cournoyer delivers the opening address at Iowa Corn Con, framing the conference as a catalyst for Midwest cyber resilience.

Key Topics: Iowa as a technology state beyond coastal innovation hubs; Corn Con's role in professional development and networking; state cyber security initiatives for local governments; and SCIM tabletop exercises for incident response.

Technical Details: Cournoyer describes state programs providing asset inventories, NIST framework assessments, and cyber security incident management exercises to local governments facing ransomware and data breach threats.

Takeaways: Regional conferences like Corn Con build cyber resilience outside major tech hubs. State government partnerships provide foundational security services to underserved local government entities.
talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Iowa Lieutenant Governor Chris Cournoyer delivers the opening keynote address at CornCon 2025 in Davenport, Iowa. Cournoyer frames the conference as a vital catalyst for regional cyber resilience, celebrating the Midwest's growing technology innovation ecosystem known as the "Silicon Prairie." She details coordinated state-level cybersecurity initiatives, critical infrastructure defense programs, and multidisciplinary educational pipelines designed to develop the next generation of cybersecurity professionals.

Key Topics:
- Midwestern technology innovation and the "Silicon Prairie" ecosystem
- Iowa Cybersecurity Resilience Initiative and public sector defense
- NIST Cybersecurity Framework integration and incident management tabletop exercises
- K-12 STEM outreach, Children of the CornCon, and workforce development

Technical Details:
Lieutenant Governor Cournoyer highlights the collaborative role of CornCon in uniting enterprise security leaders, CISOs, subject matter experts, and public sector defenders across the Quad Cities and the greater Midwest. She emphasizes that regional cybersecurity readiness requires structured coordination across municipal, county, and state entities. To operationalize this, the state launched the Iowa Cybersecurity Resilience Initiative, administered through Iowa State University’s Center for Cybersecurity Innovation and Outreach (CIO) and funded by the federal State and Local Cybersecurity Grant Program.

The initiative delivers foundational defensive capabilities to vulnerable public sector targets, including cities, counties, and school districts facing persistent threats from ransomware and data breaches. Participating entities receive standardized IT asset inventories to map attack surfaces, risk assessments aligned with the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Cybersecurity Framework, and Cybersecurity Incident Management (SCIM) tabletop exercises that simulate crisis decision-making under operational pressure. Cournoyer also announces the state’s inaugural cybersecurity conference scheduled for October 16th to sustain statewide defense momentum.

Addressing the technical workforce shortage, Cournoyer outlines Iowa’s integrated education pipeline spanning K-12 to post-graduate studies. In higher education, Iowa State University serves as a designated National Center of Academic Excellence in Cybersecurity (CAE), offering multidisciplinary programs alongside institutions such as Upper Iowa University, the University of Dubuque, and regional community colleges supported by the Future Ready Iowa Last-Dollar Scholarship. For early engagement, the Governor’s STEM Council drives the STEM BEST program and Project Lead The Way high school cybersecurity curricula. Additionally, youth-focused community initiatives like "Children of the CornCon" provide K-12 students with hands-on technical training in lockpicking, soldering, coding, Google dorking, and capture-the-flag competitions, while practical defenses like YubiKey deployments provide hardware-based multi-factor authentication (MFA) to public school IT staff.

Key Takeaways:
State and local governments must leverage structured frameworks like the NIST Cybersecurity Framework and periodic tabletop exercises to harden municipal infrastructure against ransomware. Establishing robust public-private partnerships and utilizing federal cybersecurity grants enhances defensive capabilities for resource-constrained public sector organizations. Long-term regional resilience requires proactive talent development through early STEM engagement, hands-on security education, and hardware-backed identity protections.

talks.title: CornCon_11 FRI-T1-9:00 - Lyle Kelly - The Current Threat Landscape Requires a Unique Approach
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for CornCon_11 FRI-T1-9:00 - Lyle Kelly - The Current Threat Landscape Requires a Unique Approach.
talks.summary:
Vidair Labs Overview

Lyle Kelly presents threat landscape research from Vidair Labs, a nearly decade-old Idaho research wing. The lab has found nearly 200 original vulnerabilities—59% without CVEs—and runs about 2,000 curated sandbox detonations monthly, publishing free public dashboards.

Research Methodology

Capabilities include malware sandboxes, dark web monitoring via Tor, and adversary lab environments mimicking OT, medical, IoT, and enterprise IT deployments. Honeypots invite attackers so researchers can observe exfiltration and lateral movement behaviors.

Scale of Data Exposure

Kelly cites 1.3 billion individual records leaked to date and a 2.7 billion-record host-data breach from a compromised research firm later dumped free on the dark web after failed sale attempts.

Geographic Threat Trends

Contrary to assumptions, current data shows significant exfiltration originating from U.S. infrastructure, with Russia recently leading in some metrics. Attackers abuse global hosting to launch campaigns from unexpected locations.

talks.title: CornCon_11 FRI-T2-9:00 David Garlak & Jon Schnell Chasing SSRF in Downstream Asynchronous Workflows
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning CornCon_11 FRI-T2-9:00 David Garlak & Jon Schnell Chasing SSRF in Downstream Asynchronous Workflows.
talks.summary:
SSRF Basics

David Garlak and Jon Schnell of Rapid7 define server-side request forgery as an injection point where the server fetches attacker-chosen URLs—acting as a proxy to internal or external resources. Variants include open redirects, file/SMB schemes, weak credentials, and cloud metadata misconfigurations.

Transparency Levels

They categorize transparent SSRF (attacker sees full response), semi-blind (DNS or partial hits only), and blind SSRF (no outbound visibility, requiring side channels). These labels frame later discussion of asynchronous workflows.

Defense Layers

Mitigations start with strict URL allowlisting—not denylisting—and careful URI parsing quirks. Response validation matters: teams often validate inbound input but trust fetched content. Network isolation and tight egress filtering reduce semi-blind callbacks.

Async Workflow Angle

The core topic is SSRF in downstream asynchronous jobs—webhooks, profile image fetchers, and background tasks where the request and response are decoupled. Attackers abuse delayed or blind fetches where traditional synchronous SSRF testing fails, demanding correlation across job queues and egress logs.

talks.title: CornCon_11 FRI-T3-9:45 Barry Suskind
talks.teaser: Successfully Building examines CornCon_11 FRI-T3-9:45 Barry Suskind.
talks.summary:
Purpose of tabletops

Barry Suskind at CornCon, drawing on three decades in security and SANS/Golden Institute work, frames tabletop exercises as dry-run disaster recovery for cyber incidents. They reveal gaps, stress-test teams, and teach containment of information flow so breaches are not discussed over open email or ticketing systems that could tip attackers or leak to the public.

Exercise types

Technical tabletops gather CISOs, engineers, and adjacent staff to walk through realistic scenarios inspired by current news such as ransomware. Business tabletops assume breach declaration and train executives on messaging, regulatory reporting, and crisis decisions. Combined end-to-end runs expose both sides but are hard to schedule because executives rarely sit for multi-hour sessions.

Planning essentials

Suskind recommends two- to four-hour formats, current incident response plans with accurate tooling and contact lists, clear incident command (CISO as liaison, not sole commander), separate defensive and investigative leads, and advance scheduling. He contrasts poor CrowdStrike CTO communications with stronger CEO messaging after the July outage as a lesson in public response.

talks.title: CornCon_11 FRI-T1-9:45 CISO Panel: Kevin Novak, Bruce Phillips, Paul Rice
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for CornCon_11 FRI-T1-9:45 CISO Panel: Kevin Novak, Bruce Phillips, Paul Rice.
talks.summary:
## Overview
CornCon's self-moderated CISO "ask me anything" panel (one speaker absent) shares candid views from practitioners in banking, legal, and enterprise security.

## Daily Challenges
Incident prioritization and triage dominate when every alert isn't equal. No two days match a Franklin Planner—fires constantly displace planned work. One CISO notes aerospace discipline doesn't survive modern security operations.

## Business Integration
Effective CISOs spend more time communicating up and across the business than with technology teams. A long-tenured panelist began by asking the founder "what can I do to help you?" rather than prescribing a security roadmap.

## Takeaways
Leadership, stakeholder trust, and triage judgment matter as much as tooling—invest in relationships before the next incident.

talks.title: CornCon_11 FRI-T1-10:30 - Bryan Fite - P0wning the Narrative: compelling stories...
talks.teaser: Explores how compelling narratives overshadow objective truth and what practitioners can do to defend cognitive infrastructure.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames security influence as a contest between objective facts and stories that reshape perception. He opens with a personal shift from rigid adviser to facilitator, tying trust and control to organizational confidence, then walks through point-of-origin hacking and forward-looking threat catalogs before pivoting to corporate identity fraud and an expanding attack surface of unmanaged digital identity assets.

The middle connects sales psychology, algorithmic division, deep fakes, and collaboration with the Cognitive Security Village and related institutes. He defines misinformation, disinformation, and information overload, maps sensory and cognitive attack surfaces, and contrasts fast automatic thinking with slower deliberate reasoning. Examples include conflicting public narratives and rushed judgments later contradicted by evidence.

The close offers practical responses: indicators of deceptive rhetoric, critical thinking, critical ignoring, temporal patience, pre-bunking, and immersive training through Packet Wars, the Deep Fake Justice League, and village challenges. He invites attendees to engage with published resources, awareness games, and cognitive self-defense rather than expecting a technical silver bullet.

talks.title: CornCon_11 FRI-T1-11:15
talks.teaser: A panel weighs AI tradeoffs, under-resourcing, user blame, resilience, and open debate in the security community.
talks.summary:
The session frames cybersecurity’s future as a repeating cycle: engineers ship powerful technology while defenders scramble to understand how to secure it. Mark Rorba highlights artificial intelligence and machine learning as automating mundane security work while spreading into systems whose limits are poorly understood, starting with whether sensitive data stays in-house or flows to third-party AI services. Rob Le argues the more meaningful shift is cultural—treating information security as a human discipline, with the AI boom pushing practitioners back toward that view. Win Schwarta insists the future already arrived by the 1990s, with mobile adoption in 2007 as a turning point where convenience outran risk calculation.

Asked about the next five years, the panelists see familiar problems: insufficient attention and budget, reactive industry habits, and new issues stacked on unresolved ones. Win raises who owns critical infrastructure and whether adversaries have already tested penetration, plus frank HR tension when security behaviors conflict with corporate culture. They challenge blaming end users, treating frameworks as religion without data, and vendor pitches of seamless next-generation upgrades that fix everything.

They urge viewing human and cyber elements as integrated systems, embedding security staff in real operations (mining sites, plants, cruise lines), prioritizing consequences over poorly judged risk, graceful degradation when failures are certain, and resilience such as stockpiling feed at a mine when autonomous haul trucks fail. An audience question steers toward controllable mitigations rather than impossible perfect control. The panel closes hoping the industry never loses its community—honest argument, shared support, and comfort saying “I don’t know.”

talks.title: CornCon_11 FRI-T1-12:00 - Jake Mickley
talks.teaser: Shows how autonomous pentest runs chain misconfigurations and credentials into real impact, then re-verify fixes on demand.
talks.summary:
The talk is a vendor walkthrough of an autonomous penetration testing platform, framed against traditional pentests and vulnerability scanners. The speaker argues that scheduled human tests are costly and slow to retest, while scanners list CVEs with little sense of what can actually be exploited. The platform instead focuses on exploited CVEs, misconfigurations, default settings and credential-based paths, attempts exploitation, and chains successful results to show real impact.

Several field examples were shown, each kept separate. In one environment of about 5,000 hosts, a misconfigured SMB service allowed code execution, credential dumping from a Windows security process, and escalation to domain admin, with only three machines affected. A hybrid test started on-premises with a poisoning attack, cracked a captured password hash, and then read a user's Office 365 inbox. In another case, an exposed service led to AWS keys on an adjacent Windows host, and the EDR raised no alerts. A password spray across about 100,000 hosts, using usernames gathered from LinkedIn, ended in domain compromise.

The speaker stressed assuming breach, treating credentials as a major attack path, and retesting frequently after fixes, since a Microsoft patch passed a scanner check yet remained exploitable. He recommended moving detection from alert to block, citing 77 seconds to domain compromise. Practitioners were also pointed to scheduling, an API and an MCP server for verifying specific fixes across hosts.

talks.title: CornCon_11 FRI-T1-9:45 - Fred Kwong - Deepfake 101 - How to create and spot deepfakes
talks.teaser: The session frames deepfake fraud and cost data, demos live face-swap and voice tools, and notes artifacts that expose fakes.
talks.summary:
Synthetic media has shifted from expensive, GPU-heavy production to workflows that can produce convincing clips in minutes for little or no cost. The speaker frames the risk with cost and reach figures, growth statistics, and high-profile fraud and extortion stories involving video, voice, and social distribution.

Recent capabilities include stronger realism, multimodal face modeling, live generation, and evasion that tries to defeat automated analyzers. In enterprise settings, voice cloning is called out for help-desk and impersonation scenarios, alongside survey data on public unease when content is viewed on small screens.

Most of the session is hands-on. An open-source live face-swap pipeline shows how source video, detection, alignment, and merging work, including limits on hair, skin tone, and eyeglasses. A web service turns a photo and short audio grab into a new spoken message in roughly half a minute, and a virtual-camera tool routes a face swap into conferencing software. Practitioners are urged to test these tools themselves while watching for artifacts that still leak through.

talks.title: CornCon_11 FRI-T1-4:45 - Winn Schwartau - Reframing Cognitive Defense
talks.teaser: Argues that the human mind is now an attack surface and explains how information overload and narratives shape belief.
talks.summary:
Winn Schwartau opens by framing the human mind as the new attack surface, arguing that cyber defense has long protected networks while people absorb manipulation. He describes how narratives shape belief and how too much information overwhelms decision-making, leaving people to rely on fast, habitual reactions instead of deliberate thought.

He compares the human filtering problem with signal-to-noise ratios in engineering and with biological immune systems, and introduces "critical ignoring" as a set of filters people can build and practise. He points to how bots amplify information, and describes a Cambridge study in which a gamified exercise, where participants practised creating misinformation, produced a reported 51% increase in detecting it, an approach he calls prebunking. He also proposes cognitive ranges, similar to cyber ranges, where people practise influence scenarios.

He closes by arguing that defending against cognitive attacks needs lawyers, HR staff and other non-technical disciplines alongside security teams, and points to large European public funding for cognitive defense as a sign of momentum. His takeaway is that the field is still early, research is needed on how to do this at scale, and the goal is to get people to engage slower reasoning before they act.
